doc.title: Lonnie Liston Smith interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 9, 2021

title: Not writing for hits
summary: He did not aim at gold records; Expansions and Garden of Peace took off on their own, as with Hancock and Shorter songs.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Over the years changing musical styles, I’m wondering — I’ll preface this with the fact that I’ve been playing gigs for about fifty years myself and —

And I’m always paying attention to what seems to work with different audiences. So my question I’m trying to form is have you taken into consideration the idea of trying to sell more records when you write music or create your recordings, or is that not really part of your thinking?

No. Like I said I did “Expansions” and it just took off, and then “A Garden of Peace.” Because that’s what happens, as you know the record companies put a lot of pressure on you, you know ‘cause everybody wants a gold record or a platinum record. And so that was one reason I was in the studio that day and I wrote “A Garden of Peace” I said, oh shoot, I just want to do something beautiful and peaceful. And like years later it paid off. So but I — oh Bob Thiele used to always mess with me. He said man look why don’t you call this song — what was it — Dumpy Mama or something. I said, “Bob, that’s not

cosmic, come on now.” And he’d do it on purpose, you know but like I say I was just fortunate and blessed you know that these songs just took off and stood on their own. Because Herbie Hancock, he’s written some beautiful songs, and Wayne Shorter. So I don’t think they was trying to write hits but they became hits.
Yeah. That’s the best way for it to happen I think.
